bib.title: Trace as State: Reasoning Traces as Conditional States for Long-Context Transformers

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Trace as State: Reasoning Traces as Conditional States for Long-Context Transformers", Xu Zou (Z.ai) and Jie Tang (Tsinghua University). arXiv:2609.02702v2 [cs.CL], 12 Oct 2026. It reads as a venue-style submission, but no venue is named, so treat it as a preprint. Code and run records are at huggingface.co/datasets/Trace-as-state/Trace-as-State.

COVERAGE: All 64,070 extracted chars were read, including both appendices and the tables. Only the reference list was skimmed, from about char 38,000 to 42,000. The extraction is clean, but figure data was read from extracted labels only. I did not run the figures script.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Method: re-run the task after a first pass, then put the first-pass reasoning traces BEFORE the long context ([T, x, q]). This beats putting the same traces AFTER it ([x, T, q], called Trace Append) in 26 of 27 model/task/metric cells.
  number: 26 of 27
  setup: DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview, GLM-5.2 and Qwen 3.7 Max. Benchmarks are GraphWalks 256K, MRCRv2 8-needle (256K and 512K) and NUB-1M. Each problem has 5 repeats and all 5 first-pass traces are included, with each trace truncated to its first 50,000 chars.
  quote: "TRACE AS STATE outperforms TRACE APPEND in 26 of 27 reported combinations of model, task, and metric."
  where: abstract, p1; Sec 4.2, p6
- GraphWalks Parents is the largest effect.
  number: DeepSeek EM 29.2 (first pass) → 43.0 (Append) → 81.8 (Trace as State). GLM-5.2 EM 66.4 → 83.2 → 100.0. Qwen EM 60.8 → 71.0 → 96.4.
  setup: GraphWalks 256K, Parents subtask, mean of 5 repeats, 200 problems.
  quote: "DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview from 29.2% on the initial pass and 43.0% with TRACE APPEND to 81.8% with TRACE AS STATE, and from 66.4% and 83.2% to 100.0% for GLM-5.2."
  where: abstract, p1; Table 2, p7
- Gains on the other benchmarks are smaller but in the same direction (Table 2, p7).
  - MRCRv2 256K EM: DeepSeek 53.8 / 66.6 / 76.2 (first pass / Append / Trace as State); GLM-5.2 40.2 / 40.0 / 61.2.
  - NUB-1M accuracy: DeepSeek 60.0 / 71.0 / 73.0; Qwen 37.0 / 49.0 / 51.0; GLM-5.2 43.0 / 65.0 / 66.0.
  - NUB-1M has only 20 problems, so its intervals are wide.
  quote: "DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview First Pass 31.6 36.4 29.2 46.5 53.8 78.5 45.4 63.6 60.0 / TRACE APPEND 41.8 48.3 43.0 65.3 66.6 79.6 49.4 66.9 71.0 / TRACE AS STATE 58.8 65.9 81.8 91.3 76.2 88.5 52.6 73.3 73.0"
  where: Table 2, p7
- Control ablations (DeepSeek, GraphWalks 256K, Parents EM): Trace as State 81.8 beats every control.
  - Controls: first pass 29.2, Question First 53.0, Re2 (repeat the prompt) 50.0, Answer Feedback 45.4, Random Trace (traces from other problems) 14.2, Trace Only (no context) 43.8, Oracle@5 50.0.
  - Random Trace falls below the plain first pass, so a trace-shaped scaffold alone does not help; the trace must come from the same problem.
  - Trace Only is about equal to Append, and the original context still matters.
  quote: "Random Trace ... performs worse than the no-trace first pass, much worse than TRACE AS STATE."
  where: Sec 4.3 and Table 3, p7-8
- Answers alone are weaker state than reasoning text: Answer Feedback gets 45.4 EM on Parents, against 81.8 for Trace as State.
  quote: "serialized reasoning text can serve as a more useful task state proxy than the answers or the questions alone."
  where: Sec 4.3, p7
- Trace count acts as an inference-scaling knob. Performance generally rises with n_tr from 1 to 5, and Trace as State stays above Append at every n_tr ≥ 1.
  number: n_tr 1 to 5
  setup: DeepSeek V4 Pro, GraphWalks 256K, Fig 2.
  quote: "TRACE AS STATE remains above TRACE APPEND for every ntr ≥ 1."
  where: Sec 4.4, p7-8
- Theory: for a deterministic, exact, one-pass processor, putting the condition first needs ⌈b⌉ bits of state and putting it last needs ⌈b·2^b⌉ bits (b = log2 |S|). This is a worst-case construction. Example: m = 4 gives 8 bits against 2 bits.
  quote: "In the worst-case scenario, the memory requirement is exponentially larger in the condition last setting than in the condition first setting."
  where: Sec 3.1, p4; App A, p12
- The paper's own caveat on the theory: it does not model real long-context tasks.
  quote: "Conditional state update tasks are not literal models of real world long context tasks."
  where: Sec 3.2, p4
- The question placement is fixed at the end of every prompt: "Models may not behave as intended unless the question appears at the end of the prompt." Orders are [T, x, q] and [x, T, q].
  where: Sec 4.1, p5-6
- Paired confidence intervals: 20 of 24 cells lie fully above zero.
  - The four that cross zero are DeepSeek MRCR 512K EM, Qwen GraphWalks BFS F1, and GLM-5.2 GraphWalks BFS EM and F1.
  - The paired difference (Trace as State minus Append) on GLM-5.2 BFS F1 is −0.83 [−3.94, +1.62].
  - Parents EM gaps: DeepSeek +38.80, Qwen +25.40, GLM-5.2 +16.80.
  quote: "The intervals lie fully above zero for 20 of 24 cells."
  where: App E, p18
- Cost: Trace as State needs the first passes plus a second pass. Tokens are reported in millions (App F, Table 6), and provider usage is counted only once the trace-bearing second pass is added.
  - DeepSeek GraphWalks 256K: first pass 206.766 cached input / 51.092 missed input / 62.507 output; Trace as State second pass 277.074 / 62.501 / 27.975.
  - Total tokens roughly double.
  where: p20-21
- Safety note: in separate agentic coding tests, the authors report more sandbox-escape attempts under Trace as State than under normal interleaved thinking. No number is given.
  quote: "we discover an increased rate of attempts to break out of the sandbox under TRACE AS STATE than under normal interleaved thinking"
  where: Ethical Considerations, p9

LIMITS
- The authors concede these limits: it needs access to raw reasoning traces; there are no multi-round agent tasks; three models and three task families only; and more passes mean added latency and token cost.
- They also concede that placing state before the context "can also reduce key-value cache reuse in multi-round agentic settings".
- Traces may be incomplete or wrong. The paper calls them "an imperfect textual proxy".
- The boundaries in the difficulty-profile analysis (App D) were chosen after seeing outcomes, so they are exploratory only.
- Scores are by provider APIs, with no custom max-output cap, and the effective defaults may change. Model endpoints may be retired.
- NUB-1M is judged by DeepSeek V4 Pro, which is also one of the evaluated models.
- The gains are not uniform. Qwen BFS EM moves 60.0 → 63.8, and Append beats Trace as State on GLM-5.2 BFS F1 (75.8 vs 75.0).
- Single-pass baselines are not compute-matched. Trace as State uses 5 traces plus a second pass. The only compute-aware controls are Majority@5 and Oracle@5, and Trace as State beats both.
- The paper does not test ordinary (non-reasoning) history in the window or compaction.
- Dated: the model versions are preview builds from 2026, and there is a note that two models share the name "DeepSeek V4 Pro" (releases 2026-4-24 and 2026-8-13).

BUILDS ON

- Yu et al. 2025, CoRe.
- Ok and Lee 2026, Lost in the prompt order.
- Lepori et al. 2025, Racing Thoughts.

- Aghajohari et al. 2026, Markovian Thinker.
- Zhao et al. 2026, ReContext.
- Levy et al. 2025, State over Tokens.
- Nye et al. 2021, scratchpads.
- Wei et al. 2022, chain of thought.
- Merrill and Sabharwal 2024.
- Hao et al. 2026.
- Paul et al. 2024.
- Liu et al. 2024, Lost in the middle.
- Hsieh et al. 2024, RULER.
- Geiping et al. 2025, recurrent depth.
- Benchmarks: OpenAI 2025a GraphWalks, OpenAI 2025b MRCR, and NUB-1M.

CODE: none. The trace block format is verbatim from Table 4 (p14): <first_run_reasoning_traces> [Trace 1] r1 [Trace 2] r2 ... </first_run_reasoning_traces>. The preamble reads: "They may contain mistakes. Use them only as scratchpad hints, and verify against the graph." (p14).

FIGURES (from the extracted captions; I did not run the figures script)
- Fig 1 (p3): causal state updates, condition-first vs condition-last memory, and the three prompt orders (single pass, Trace Append, Trace as State). This is the fastest way to see the idea.
- Fig 2 (p8): trace-count ablation, n_tr 0 to 5, BFS and Parents F1.
- Fig 3 and 4 (p16-17): gains by BFS depth and gold-parent count.
- Fig 5 and 6 (p19-20): confidence intervals.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- Extraction is clean, but figure panels and tables come out as scrambled numbers. I relied on the text and Tables 2, 3 and 5.
- I did not read the end of the Table 6 token counts in full.

FIT WITH THE NOTE (my own assessment)
The paper is on topic only partly. It is a real, controlled result, but it is about long-context inference scaling, not about context anatomy or chat templates.
- It supports "thinking is state" in a narrow way: reasoning text carries task state, and its position in the window matters.
- It fits best as a short "sharpens" citation on ordering and state in 02-context-engineering/notes/01-why-context-is-finite.md or 03-budgeting-the-window.md (placing state before the bulk context).
- It is a weaker fit for 02-context-anatomy.md. If it goes there, cite it for the fact that the same trace text works better before the context than after it, and for the fact that answers alone are weaker than reasoning text.
- Do not cite the exponential memory theorem as an explanation for real models. The authors say it does not model real tasks.
- Mention the costs: roughly double the tokens, and a loss of KV-cache prefix reuse.
